Technical words in the series link here, usually the first time they appear on a page. Each entry gives a plain definition and a link to a fuller explanation.

## Sound

[Hertz (Hz)]{#hertz}
: One cycle per second, the unit of frequency. The A above middle C is tuned to 440 Hz. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hertz)

[Periodic]{#periodic}
: A signal $p(t)$ is periodic with period $P > 0$ if it repeats exactly every $P$ seconds: $p(t + P) = p(t)$ for all $t$. Its *shortest* such $P$ is usually what is meant by the period. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Periodic_function)

[Pitch]{#pitch}
: How high or low a note sounds. For a periodic sound with shortest period $P$, the pitch is heard at the repetition rate $1/P$, even when no component at that frequency is present, as long as that rate is between a few dozen and a few thousand per second. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pitch_(music)), and [page 0](note.qmd)

[Partial, overtone]{#partial}
: A sound can be split into components of single frequencies; each one is a partial. An overtone is any partial above the lowest. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overtone)

[Fundamental]{#fundamental}
: For a periodic sound, the frequency $f = 1/P$ at which it repeats; its harmonics are the whole-number multiples of $f$. It is usually the lowest and strongest partial, but it can be weak or even missing, and the pitch is still heard at $f$ ([page 0](note.qmd)). For a sound that is not periodic, such as a drum's, "fundamental" just means the lowest partial. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fundamental_frequency)

[Harmonic]{#harmonic}
: A partial at a whole-number multiple $nf$ of the fundamental. A periodic sound contains only harmonics. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmonic)

[Harmonic series]{#harmonic-series}
: The whole-number multiples $f, 2f, 3f, \dots$ of one frequency $f$. All the partials of a periodic sound belong to one harmonic series. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmonic_series_(music))

[Inharmonic]{#inharmonic}
: Having partials that are not whole-number multiples of one frequency. A bell, a drum and a kalimba tine are strongly inharmonic; a piano string is slightly inharmonic. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inharmonicity)

[Timbre]{#timbre}
: What tells two notes of the same pitch and loudness apart, such as a violin and a flute both playing A. It depends mostly on the relative strengths of the partials and how they change over the course of the note. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Timbre)

[Note names: C4, A4, middle C]{#note-names}
: Notes are named by a letter from A to G and an octave number. C4 is middle C, about 262 Hz, near the middle of the piano keyboard; C5 is the C an octave above it; A4 is the A at 440 Hz. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scientific_pitch_notation)

[Semitone]{#semitone}
: The smallest step on a piano, from one key to the next, white or black. Twelve semitones make an octave. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semitone)

[Equal temperament]{#equal-temperament}
: The usual way of tuning a piano: every semitone is the same frequency ratio, $2^{1/12} \approx 1.0595$, so twelve of them make an exact octave. The price is that the other intervals miss the simple ratios slightly: an equal-tempered fifth is $2^{7/12} \approx 1.4983$, not $3/2$. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equal_temperament)

[Cent]{#cents}
: A unit for small differences in pitch: one hundredth of an equal-tempered semitone, so an octave is 1200 cents. Two frequencies in the ratio $r$ are $1200\log_2 r$ cents apart. Trained listeners notice a few cents. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cent_(music))

[Octave, fifth, twelfth]{#octave}
: Musical intervals, named by frequency ratio. An octave is a ratio of 2. A fifth is the ratio $3/2$ when tuned to the simple ratio, and $2^{7/12} \approx 1.498$ in equal temperament. A twelfth, an octave plus a fifth, is about 3. Smaller intervals, by their simple ratios: the minor third $6/5$, the major third $5/4$, the fourth $4/3$ and the major sixth $5/3$. Two notes an octave apart sound like "the same note, higher". [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interval_(music))

[Beats]{#beats}
: When two pure tones of nearly equal frequency sound together, their sum swells and fades in loudness at a rate equal to the difference of their frequencies. Tuners listen for beats; fast beats are heard as roughness. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beat_(acoustics))

[Consonance, roughness]{#consonance}
: Consonance is how smooth or stable two notes sound together. Roughness is one ingredient of it: the harsh quality of fast beats between partials that are close but not equal. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Consonance_and_dissonance), and the [epilogue](epilogue.qmd)

## Instrument parts and playing

[Nut, bridge]{#bridge}
: On a string instrument, the two points that end a string's vibrating length: the nut at the top of the neck, the bridge on the body. The bridge also carries the string's vibration to the body, or on a piano to the soundboard. On a kalimba, the bridge is the bar the tines are pressed against. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bridge_(instrument))

[Open string]{#open-string}
: A string played with no finger pressing it down, so its whole length between the nut and the bridge vibrates. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Open_string_(music))

[Harmonics, on a string]{#string-harmonics}
: Notes a string player gets by touching the string lightly at a fraction of its length, such as the middle, instead of pressing it down. Only the modes with a still point under the finger keep sounding. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/String_harmonic), and [page 4](violin.qmd)

[Overblowing, register key]{#overblow}
: Making a wind instrument's air column jump to a higher mode. A flutist overblows by blowing faster; a clarinetist presses the register key, which opens a small hole that spoils the lowest mode. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Overblowing), and [page 5](clarinet.qmd)

[Blow, draw]{#draw}
: On a harmonica, a blow note sounds when you breathe out through a hole, and a draw note when you breathe in. Each hole has one reed for each (on a chromatic harmonica, one for each in each of its two sets). [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harmonica)

[Free reed]{#free-reed}
: A thin metal tongue fixed at one end that swings through a closely fitting slot, opening and shutting it like a valve. Harmonicas and accordions use free reeds. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Free_reed_aerophone)

[Damper]{#damper}
: A felt pad that rests on a piano string and stops it when the key is released. Each key lifts its own damper while held; the right pedal lifts them all. The highest strings, roughly the top 20 keys, have no dampers. [Wikipedia: Sustain pedal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sustain_pedal)

[Soft pedal, una corda]{#soft-pedal}
: The left pedal of a piano. On a grand it shifts the hammers sideways so they hit fewer strings; this is the *una corda*, Italian for "one string". On an upright it instead moves the hammers closer to the strings, so they strike more gently. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Soft_pedal)

[Practice pedal, mute]{#practice-pedal}
: The middle pedal on many uprights. It lowers a strip of felt between the hammers and the strings, making the sound much quieter and duller. [Wikipedia: Piano pedals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piano_pedals)

## Vibration

[Partial derivative, $u_t$, $u_{xx}$]{#partial-derivative}
: For a function of several variables, such as the height $u(x, t)$ of a string at position $x$ and time $t$, the rate of change in one variable with the others held fixed. Subscripts name the variable: $u_t$ is the velocity of the point at $x$, $u_{tt}$ its acceleration, $u_x$ the slope of the string, and $u_{xx}$ how fast that slope changes along it, which for small slopes is its curvature. Mixed subscripts mean one derivative after another: $u_{xt}$ is the rate of change in $t$ of the slope $u_x$; for a smooth function the order does not matter, $u_{xt} = u_{tx}$. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partial_derivative)

[Proportional, $\propto$]{#proportional}
: $a \propto b$ means that $a$ is a fixed number times $b$. So $f \propto 1/L^2$ means that halving $L$ multiplies $f$ by four. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proportionality_(mathematics))

[Angular frequency]{#angular-frequency}
: $\omega = 2\pi f$: the frequency counted in radians per second instead of cycles per second, one cycle being $2\pi$ radians. Formulas such as $\omega^2 = k/m$ are shortest in $\omega$. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angular_frequency)

[Wavenumber]{#wavenumber}
: The counterpart of angular frequency in space: a wave $\sin kx$ has wavenumber $k = 2\pi/\text{wavelength}$. For the wave equation, $\omega = ck$. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wavenumber)

[Linear]{#linear}
: An equation with no outside force is linear if sums and multiples of solutions are again solutions. An equation with an outside force is linear when it reads (left side) = (the force), where the force does not involve $u$, and the left side is built from $u$ and its derivatives only by multiplying each by a number, or by a given function of position and time, and adding: no $u^2$, no $u\,u_x$, no $\sin u$. The [piano page](piano.qmd)'s $\mu u_{tt} + b\,u_t - Tu_{xx} + EI\,u_{xxxx} = f(x, t)$ is an example. Then the difference of any two solutions solves the same equation without the force. The operators in this series are linear, a good model for the small vibrations of instruments. What keeps a bowed string, a clarinet reed or a harmonica reed going is not linear: the bow's grip and slip and a reed opening and closing. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_differential_equation)

[Superposition]{#superposition}
: Adding solutions of a linear equation to get another solution. The free motion of an instrument, once nothing is driving it, is a superposition, a sum, of its modes. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Superposition_principle)

[Mode, normal mode]{#mode}
: A motion of an object, with no friction and nothing driving it, in which every part swings at the same single frequency and the overall shape stays the same, only growing and shrinking. Every small free vibration is a sum of modes. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal_mode)

[Standing wave]{#standing-wave}
: A wave whose shape stays in place, such as a mode of a string. It can be seen as two equal waves traveling in opposite directions. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Standing_wave)

[Node, antinode, nodal line]{#node}
: A node is a point of a standing wave that does not move; an antinode is a point that moves the most. Touching a string lightly at a node of a mode does not disturb that mode. On a drumhead or a plate, a mode stays still along whole curves, its nodal lines; Chladni's sand collects on them. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Node_(physics))

[Wave equation]{#wave-equation}
: The equation $u_{tt} = c^2u_{xx}$ for the height $u(x, t)$ of a stretched string, and its relatives for air in a pipe and for a drumhead. The constant $c$ is the speed at which a bump travels. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wave_equation), and [page 3](circle.qmd)

[Boundary condition]{#boundary-condition}
: A rule for what happens at the edge of a vibrating object, set by how it is held. A string tied down at an end has $u = 0$ there. A bar clamped at an end can neither move nor tilt there: $u = 0$ and $u_x = 0$. At the open end of a pipe the pressure equals room pressure. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boundary_value_problem), and [page 4](violin.qmd)

[Dirichlet and Neumann conditions]{#dirichlet}
: Two kinds of boundary condition. A Dirichlet condition fixes the value at the edge, such as $u = 0$ at a string's tied end or $p = 0$ at a pipe's open end. A Neumann condition fixes the slope, such as $p_x = 0$ at a clarinet's reed end. [Wikipedia: Dirichlet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_boundary_condition), [Neumann](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neumann_boundary_condition)

[Damping]{#damping}
: Friction that drains energy from a vibration, so that it dies away. A term $b\,u_t$ in the equation, proportional to velocity, is the simplest model. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Damping)

[Self-sustained oscillation, limit cycle]{#self-sustained}
: An oscillation kept going at a steady size by a steady supply of energy, such as a bow drawn at constant speed or a steady breath. In normal playing the motion settles into one repeating cycle, called a limit cycle; under some conditions it does not, as in the unsteady, warbling *wolf note* of some cellos. This needs a mechanism that is not linear, such as the bow's grip and slip or a reed opening and closing. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-oscillation)

[Coupling]{#coupling}
: Two vibrating parts are coupled when the motion of one pushes on the other, as when piano strings share a bridge. Coupled parts trade energy, and their modes mix. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Coupling_(physics))

[Helmholtz motion]{#helmholtz-motion}
: The way a bowed string moves. The string sticks to the bow, slips back, and sticks again; seen from the side, a single sharp corner races back and forth along the string, one round trip per period. [J. Wolfe, UNSW: The bowed string](https://newt.phys.unsw.edu.au/jw/Bows.html)

[Cantilever, clamped bar]{#cantilever}
: A bar fixed rigidly at one end, so that end can neither move nor tilt, and free at the other, like a diving board. A kalimba tine is close to a cantilever: it is pressed against a bridge near one end and its tip is free. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cantilever)

[Euler–Bernoulli beam]{#beam}
: The standard model of a bending bar under no tension: $\mu u_{tt} = -EI\,u_{xxxx}$, where $\mu$ is the mass per unit length, $E$ the [Young's modulus](#youngs-modulus) and $I$ the [second moment of area](#second-moment). The bar resists being bent, and bending is curvature, two derivatives; balancing forces along the bar adds two more, giving four. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler%E2%80%93Bernoulli_beam_theory)

[Bending moment, shear force]{#moment}
: Imagine cutting a bent bar at some point. The bending moment is the turning effect that one side exerts on the other, which tries to bend the bar; the shear force is the sideways force across the cut. A free end carries neither. [Wikipedia: Bending moment](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bending_moment), [Shear force](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shear_force)

[Young's modulus]{#youngs-modulus}
: How stiff a material is when stretched: the force per unit area needed, divided by the fraction by which it lengthens. Steel is about 200 GPa; nylon, used for classical guitar strings, is a few GPa. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Young%27s_modulus)

[Second moment of area]{#second-moment}
: How the shape of a bar's cross-section resists bending, written $I$. For a rectangle of width $w$ and thickness $h$, $I = wh^3/12$: doubling the thickness makes the bar eight times harder to bend. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_moment_of_area)

[Hyperbolic functions, cosh and sinh]{#hyperbolic}
: $\cosh x = (e^x + e^{-x})/2$ and $\sinh x = (e^x - e^{-x})/2$. They satisfy $\cosh^2 x - \sinh^2 x = 1$, much as $\cos^2 + \sin^2 = 1$. Differentiating the definitions gives $(\cosh x)' = \sinh x$ and $(\sinh x)' = \cosh x$, with no sign change, and $\cosh 0 = 1$, $\sinh 0 = 0$. In a bar they describe the part of the bending that grows or fades along the bar instead of wiggling. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyperbolic_functions)

[Bulk modulus, adiabatic]{#bulk-modulus}
: How hard a material is to compress: the pressure needed, divided by the fraction by which the volume shrinks. In a sound wave the squeezes are too quick for heat to flow in or out, which is called adiabatic, and for air this gives about $1.4 \times$ atmospheric pressure. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bulk_modulus)

[First-order approximation]{#first-order}
: Keeping only the terms proportional to a small change and dropping those proportional to its square and higher powers. For a small $\varepsilon$, $(1 + \varepsilon)^3 = 1 + 3\varepsilon + 3\varepsilon^2 + \varepsilon^3 \approx 1 + 3\varepsilon$ to first order. A second-order approximation keeps the $\varepsilon^2$ terms too. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Perturbation_theory)

## Matrices and operators

[Matrix times vector]{#matrix-vector}
: For a square matrix $K$ and a list of numbers $v$, the product $Kv$ is the list whose $j$-th entry is $\sum_k K_{jk}v_k$: row $j$ of $K$, multiplied entry by entry with $v$ and added up. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matrix_multiplication)

[Eigenvector, eigenvalue]{#eigenvector}
: A nonzero vector $v$ that a matrix $K$ only rescales, multiplying it by a number $\lambda$: $Kv = \lambda v$. The number $\lambda$ is the eigenvalue. On the bead ring of [page 2](ring.qmd), $v$ lists how far each bead is displaced and $Kv$ the forces pulling them back, up to a constant; an eigenvector is a shape in which each bead is pulled back in proportion to its own displacement, so all the beads swing at one frequency. Eigenvalues are squared angular frequencies, up to a constant. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eigenvalues_and_eigenvectors)

[Eigenvalue]{#eigenvalue}
: See [eigenvector](#eigenvector).

[Multiplicity]{#multiplicity}
: The number of independent eigenvectors that share one eigenvalue. Vectors are *independent* when none of them is a combination of the others. On a ring, the cosine and sine shapes of the same wave are two independent modes with the same frequency, so that frequency has multiplicity 2. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eigenvalues_and_eigenvectors#Geometric_multiplicity)

[Perpendicular, orthogonal]{#orthogonal}
: Two vectors are perpendicular, or orthogonal, when their dot product, the sum of the products of matching entries, is zero. For functions the dot product is replaced by the [inner product](#inner-product). [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Orthogonality_(mathematics))

[Symmetric matrix]{#symmetric-matrix}
: A square matrix of real numbers equal to its own mirror image across the diagonal: the entry in row $i$, column $j$ equals the entry in row $j$, column $i$. The spectral theorem says its eigenvalues are real and it has a full set of perpendicular eigenvectors. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectral_theorem)

[Determinant]{#determinant}
: A number computed from a square matrix that is zero exactly when the matrix sends some nonzero vector to zero. So linear equations with all right-hand sides zero have a solution other than all zeros exactly when the determinant of their coefficients is zero. For a $2\times2$ matrix with rows $(p, q)$ and $(r, s)$ it is $ps - qr$. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Determinant)

[Circulant matrix]{#circulant}
: A square matrix in which each row is the row above shifted one place to the right, wrapping around. Whatever its entries, the complex waves $e^{2\pi ijk/N}$ of the discrete Fourier transform, the next entry, are eigenvectors of it; when the matrix is also symmetric, as on page 2, so are the real cosine and sine waves. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Circulant_matrix)

[Discrete Fourier transform (DFT)]{#dft}
: Writing a list of $N$ numbers, indexed by $j = 0, \dots, N-1$, as a sum of the waves $\cos(2\pi jk/N)$ and $\sin(2\pi jk/N)$ for $k = 0, \dots, N-1$; with [Euler's formula](#euler-formula) these are combined into $e^{2\pi ijk/N}$. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discrete_Fourier_transform), and [page 2](ring.qmd)

[Euler's formula]{#euler-formula}
: $e^{i\theta} = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta$, where $i^2 = -1$. It packs a cosine and a sine into one expression that is easier to multiply and differentiate. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler%27s_formula)

[Operator]{#operator}
: A rule that takes a function and returns another function. In this series the operator $A$ takes a shape $u$ of the instrument (for air in a tube, its pressure) and returns minus its acceleration: for a string or a bar, minus the restoring force per unit mass. So the motion obeys $u_{tt} = -Au$. The operator includes its constant, for example $A = -c^2\,d^2/dx^2$ for a string with $c^2 = T/\mu$, and comes with its allowed shapes, those that obey the boundary conditions. All of these operators are linear. Each eigenvalue $\lambda$ of $A$ gives a frequency $\sqrt{\lambda}/2\pi$. The idea is laid out on [The spectrum of an operator](spectrum.qmd). [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operator_(mathematics))

[Eigenfunction]{#eigenfunction}
: A nonzero function $f$ that an operator only rescales: $Af = \lambda f$. Example: $-\frac{d^2}{d\theta^2}\cos 3\theta = 9\cos 3\theta$. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eigenfunction)

[Spectrum]{#spectrum}
: For every instrument in this series, the list of its operator's eigenvalues $\lambda$; the frequencies are $\sqrt{\lambda}/2\pi$. (In general, for an operator on an infinite-dimensional space, the spectrum is the set of numbers $\lambda$ for which $A - \lambda$ has no well-behaved inverse, which can contain more than eigenvalues.) See [The spectrum of an operator](spectrum.qmd). [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spectrum_(functional_analysis))

[Inner product]{#inner-product}
: A way to multiply two vectors or two functions to get a number, generalizing the dot product. For functions on the circle, $\langle f, g\rangle = \int_0^{2\pi} f\,\bar g\,d\theta$, where $\bar g$ is the complex conjugate of $g$, which is just $g$ when $g$ is real. Two functions are perpendicular if it is zero. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Inner_product_space)

[$L^2(S^1)$]{#l2}
: The space of functions on the circle $S^1$ with $\int_0^{2\pi}|f|^2\,d\theta$ finite, with the inner product above. (For readers who know measure theory: two functions that differ only on a set of measure zero count as the same.) It is where the shapes of a vibrating loop live. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lp_space)

[Symmetric and self-adjoint operators]{#self-adjoint}
: An operator $A$ is symmetric if $\langle Af, g\rangle = \langle f, Ag\rangle$ for all allowed $f$ and $g$, the analogue of a symmetric matrix. That alone makes its eigenvalues real and its eigenfunctions for different eigenvalues perpendicular. Self-adjoint is a stronger condition on the set of allowed shapes, roughly that it is neither too small nor too large. Together with a further property that every instrument here has, it is what the spectral theorem needs to give enough eigenfunctions to build every shape ([page 3](circle.qmd)). (For readers who know functional analysis: self-adjoint means $A = A^*$, domains included; for the loop the domain is $H^2(S^1)$, and the further property is that $(A + 1)^{-1}$ is compact.) [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Self-adjoint_operator)

[Fourier series]{#fourier-series}
: Writing a periodic function as a sum of sines and cosines, or of $e^{in\theta}$, of whole-number frequencies. On [page 3](circle.qmd) this is the expansion in eigenfunctions of $-d^2/d\theta^2$. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fourier_series)

[Laplacian]{#laplacian}
: The operator $\Delta u = u_{xx} + u_{yy}$ in the plane. At each point it is proportional to how far $u$ sits below the average of its values on a small circle around the point. A drumhead's operator is $-c^2\Delta$. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laplace_operator)

[Separation of variables]{#separation-of-variables}
: Looking for solutions that are a product of a function of one variable and a function of another, such as $u(x, t) = X(x)\,q(t)$. It splits one equation in several variables into simpler equations in one variable each. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Separation_of_variables)

[Bessel function]{#bessel}
: The functions $J_m(r)$ that describe how the modes of a round drum vary from the center to the rim, as sines do along a string. $J_0$ starts at 1 and swings like a slowly fading cosine, crossing zero at $r \approx 2.405,\ 5.520,\ 8.654, \dots$; for $m \ge 1$, $J_m$ starts at 0. Their zeros, which are not whole-number multiples of the first one, set the drum's frequencies. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bessel_function), and [page 8](drum.qmd)

[Divergence theorem]{#divergence-theorem}
: The total flow out through the boundary of a region equals the sum, over the region, of how much flow is created at each point. It turns forces along the edge of a patch of drumhead into an integral over the patch. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divergence_theorem)

[Rayleigh quotient]{#rayleigh-quotient}
: The ratio of a shape's stored energy to its mass-weighted size, for example $R(f) = \int EI\,(f'')^2\,dx \big/ \int \rho S\,f^2\,dx$ for a bar; for a shape that meets all the boundary conditions it equals $\langle Af, f\rangle/\langle f, f\rangle$. Its smallest value, over all nonzero shapes $f$ that obey the conditions at clamped or fixed ends, is the lowest eigenvalue, reached at the lowest mode; in this energy form, conditions at free ends need not be imposed. It explains why removing metal near the base of a reed or tine lowers its pitch and removing it near the tip raises it. [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rayleigh_quotient)

## Shape and spectrum

[Weyl's law]{#weyl}
: For a drum of area $|\Omega|$, the number $N(\Lambda)$ of eigenvalues of $-\Delta$ below a large number $\Lambda$ is close to $|\Omega|\Lambda/4\pi$, so the spectrum "hears" the area. A second term, $-P\sqrt\Lambda/4\pi$ with $P$ the perimeter, is proved only under extra conditions, but for drums with smooth or polygonal rims the perimeter can be heard anyway, by a smoother count ([page 9](shape.qmd)). [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weyl_law)

[Isospectral]{#isospectral}
: Having the same spectrum, counted with multiplicity. Gordon, Webb and Wolpert found two differently shaped drums that are isospectral. [Wikipedia: Hearing the shape of a drum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hearing_the_shape_of_a_drum)
